name: Tzeltal
confidence_why: Polian 2013 (the reference grammar of Oxchuc Tseltal), Gerdel 1974 and Smith 1999 all put the accent on the final syllable, of the phonological phrase in Polian's analysis, but Kaufman 1971, known only through the Stanford Phonology Archive digest of 1979 and Shklovsky 2005, treats word-level stress as root-initial with the final prominence being phrasal, and Bennett 2016 notes that whether Tseltal has word-level stress at all is unsettled.
sweep_summary: The one works with stress in the title, Shklovsky 2011 'Petalcingo Tseltal intonational prosody' (FAMLi I, MITWPL 63: 209-220), is a print-only paid volume (MITWPL catalog page downloaded; no open copy on lingbuzz, IA Scholar, BASE, the Internet Archive; by its title and the way Shklovsky 2012 and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 cite it, it is about boundary tones (H% on declaratives/wh-questions, L% on polar questions), not word-stress placement; medium priority. Three open sources were newly downloaded from archive.org and read: Gerdel 1974 'Tzeltal (Mayan) phonemes' section 1.4 (first-hand: final stress on the stress/pause group, secondary initial stress, Spanish penult loans unshifted), the Stanford Phonology Archive 1979 entry summarizing Kaufman 1971 (root-morpheme stress, affixes unstressed, primary stress only phrase-finally; this is the source of the 'word-initial' counter-claim, and it contradicts a word-level fixed: final syllable coding), and the Spanish original of Smith's manual (same 'always last syllable' statement); the 1957 Chicago 'El Tzeltal Hablado' course is silent. Polian 2013 (held by the project under tzel1255) remains the best first-hand statement: fixed final accent at the phonological-phrase level, realized by F0 rise and lengthening, with listed loan exceptions and root-initial emphatic lengthening; it should replace the Wikipedia/Smith citation and the domain should be coded phrase, with Kaufman 1971 (still unread, archive.org lending only) as the high-priority acquisition.

new_statements.quote: El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas, que se pueden caracterizar aproximativamente como los constituyentes prosódicos que agrupan un núcleo léxico y todos sus satélites [...] si una palabra viene seguida de clíticos, estos se integran a la misma frase fonológica que la palabra anterior y pueden por lo tanto llevar el acento final
new_statements.translation: Tseltal is a fixed-accent language (Kager 2007), and so has no lexically contrastive accent as Spanish does. The accent falls on the last syllable of phonological phrases, and in particular at the end of the utterance. [...] The final accent does not properly concern words but phonological phrases, which can be roughly characterized as the prosodic constituents grouping a lexical head and all its satellites [...] if a word is followed by clitics, these join the same phonological phrase as the preceding word and can therefore carry the final accent
new_statements.citation: Polian, Gilles (2013). Gramática del tseltal de Oxchuc, Tomo I. México: CIESAS (Publicaciones de la Casa Chata). Section 3.2 'Acento y prosodia', pp. 85-87 (and 3.8.10, p. 123).
new_statements.reading: Fixed final accent, but the domain is the phonological phrase (utterance-final above all), realized by an F0 rise plus vowel lengthening rather than intensity; non-final phrases need not be accented; clitics carry it; roots additionally take an emphatic initial-syllable lengthening (stronger in Bachajón); exceptions: Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans with initial accent, V-final Spanish loans with penult ~ final. Corroborated first-hand this search of works with stress in the title by Gerdel 1974 section 1.4 p. 103 (final stress on the stress group = pause group, secondary stress on the initial syllable, Spanish penult loans unshifted; newly downloaded open copy at and, at second hand, the SPA 1979 digest of Kaufman 1971 (root-morpheme stress, primary only phrase-finally), which is the competing word-level analysis. Keep classification fixed-dominant final non-strict; set domain phrase; cite Polian 2013 I:85-87, 123 with Gerdel 1974 as corroboration.

tone_statements.quote: Le tseltal n’étant en aucun cas une langue à tons, ni à accent intoné28, nous parlerons de tonalité vocalique plutôt que ton. ... On retiendra donc de ces mesures l’importance de normaliser les valeurs de F0, et la non incidence de la réarticulation et de la gémination sur le contour interne du noyau complexe – autrement dit, l’absence de corrélation tonale de ces réflexes.
tone_statements.translation: Since Tseltal is in no way a tone language, nor a pitch-accent language, we will speak of vocalic tonality rather than tone. ... From these measurements we retain the importance of normalising F0 values, and the absence of any effect of rearticulation and gemination on the internal contour of the complex nucleus – in other words, the absence of a tonal correlation for these reflexes.
tone_statements.locator: §4.1.4 'Tonalité de la voyelle basse réarticulée GLOT.OUV.', HAL author-version pp. 29-30; fn. 28 on p. 29 cites Kaufman 1998 for low tones in San Bartolo Tsotsil
tone_statements.summary: States Tseltal has neither tone nor pitch accent; F0 measurements of VhV/V'V nuclei across 17 localities show no tonal correlate or tonogenesis (contrast fn. 28: low tones in San Bartolo Tsotsil).

readall_conflicts: No new first-hand statement was obtained, so no new conflict arises. The standing tension held by the project remains: the catalog (an earlier compilation, corroborated first-hand by Polian 2013 pp. 85-87 and Gerdel 1974 p. 103) codes Tzeltal as fixed final accent with the phonological phrase as domain, while Kaufman 1971, known only through the SPA 1979 digest (Kaufman pp. 9, 24-29), analyses stress as a property of root morphemes (affixes stressless) with primary stress realized phrase-finally and secondary stress elsewhere; the two agree on phrase-final primary prominence and differ on whether roots carry an underlying word-level stress. Resolving Kaufman's exact rule needs the book itself (archive.org loan or Harvard scan-and-deliver).

audit.recode_to: Keep classification fixed-dominant (final, non-strict); change domain not yet coded -> phrase per Polian 2013 p. 86 ('El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas'); cite Polian 2013 I:85-87, 123 as deciding source with Smith MS as corroboration; add caution: root-initial lengthening prominence (Polian fn. 2, stronger in Bachajón) and Kaufman 1971 reportedly describing word-initial word stress (Shklovsky 2005), Bennett 2016 / DiCanio & Bennett 2018 treating word- vs phrase-level status as unresolved; exceptions listed-set (V-final Spanish loans penult ~ final; Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans initial).

sources.quote: El tseltal es una lengua de acento fijo (Kager, 2007), y por lo mismo no presenta un acento léxicamente contrastivo como el español. El acento recae sobre la última sílaba de las frases fonológicas, y en particular al final del enunciado. [...] El acento final no concierne propiamente las palabras, sino las frases fonológicas [...] si una palabra viene seguida de clíticos, estos se integran a la misma frase fonológica que la palabra anterior y pueden por lo tanto llevar el acento final (p. 85-86) [...] las raíces léxicas pueden, además, recibir un acento de énfasis en su sílaba inicial, que se realiza sólo mediante un alargamiento de la vocal (p. 87)
sources.note: Fixed accent on the last syllable of the phonological phrase (not the word), realized by F0 rise and vowel lengthening, not intensity; non-final phrases need not be accented; clitics take the final accent (Kerem-at=to=lá); lexical roots additionally take an emphatic initial-syllable lengthening, stronger in Bachajón than Oxchuc (fn. 2); Mixe-Zoquean CVCV loans have lexical initial accent (áko, páta, tsíma, fn. 1); Spanish loans: C-final ones become oxytone (axúx, wakáx), V-final ones keep penult stress alternating with final (káxa ~ kaxá) (p. 123). Refines the catalog: final position confirme…

sources.citation: Gerdel, Florence L. (1974). Tzeltal (Mayan) phonemes. SIL Mexico Workpapers 1: 101-106 (Oxchuc dialect; MS dated Sept. 1955). Section 1.4 Stress, p. 103 (p. 3).
sources.quote: Stress in Tzeltal may best be described in terms of stress groups. A stress group is a stretch of speech of two or more syllables with a unifying stress on the final syllable (indicated in this paper by acute accent over the vowel); and, in stress groups of more than two syllables, a secondary stress on the first or second syllable (indicated in this paper by grave accent over the vowel). Stressed syllables are normally higher in pitch than unstressed syllables. In most cases, the stress group is synonymous with a pause group, defined as a stretch of speech between pauses. [...] Stress groups of two syllables have the stress on the final syllable. This is called pattern I: patil 'later', talon 'I came', pasp'il 'made'.
sources.locator: section 1.4, p. 103 (article pp. 101-106; PDF page 3, lines ~165-200)
sources.note: First-hand SIL description of Oxchuc Tzeltal: primary stress on the final syllable of the stress group (= pause group, i.e. a phrase, not the word), secondary stress on the first syllable (or second, when the first syllable is an 'innately unstressed' particle such as ya, a-, te); stressed syllables are higher in pitch; pattern IV (emphasis) reverses to initial stress; 'in words of Spanish origin, the Spanish stress pattern predominates in that Spanish words with penultimate stress normally do not shift stress', with occasional nativized pesu ~ pesu, semana, limeta; two native exceptions ?ili…

sources.citation: Shklovsky, Kirill. 2005. Person Marking in Petalcingo Tzeltal. BA thesis, Reed College. Chapter 1: A grammatical sketch of Petalcingo Tzeltal.
sources.quote: 'Stress is one of the phenomena in Petalcingo Tzeltal that is still quite obscure to me. While Haviland (p.c.) suggests that stress in Mayan languages like Tzotzil and Tzeltal falls on the root, Kaufman 1971 and p.c. argues that word-stress in Tzeltal is word-initial. In my experience, clause-level (prosodic stress) in Petalcingo Tzeltal serves to at least partially obscure word-level stress.'

sources.quote: Declarative utterances and wh-questions in Petalcingo end on a high tone (Shklovsky 2011), and topics do so as well. Petalcingo topics bear the H% boundary tone even when the CP with which they are interpreted itself is associated with a low boundary tone

sources.citation: Smith, Joshua Hinmán. n.d. [Eng. tr. 1999]. Manual of Spoken Tzeltal. Translated by Stuart P. Robinson, ed. Madelief Bertens. MS distributed via tzeltal.org (the Internet Archive 2006 snapshot).
sources.quote: 'stress always falls on the last syllable of a word. For example, one says ch'ahíl ("smoke") and t'uyúy ("passionfruit"). If a root takes a suffix or if it follows a particle, the accent falls on the latter. For example, bah é ... or tal íx ... Many loan-words retain penultimate stress in the Spanish style (e.g., lóbleh, "oak"), but the older loans have undergone a shift of stress to the final syllable (e.g., markúx, "Marcus").'

sources.citation: Crothers, John H., James P. Lorentz, Donald A. Sherman & Marilyn M. Vihman (eds.) (1979). Handbook of Phonological Data from a Sample of the World's Languages: A Report of the Stanford Phonology Archive, vol. 1, entry 805 Tzeltal, pp. 417-419 (a summary of Kaufman 1971, Tzeltal phonology and morphology, UCPL 61).
sources.quote: STRESS: Phrase and sentence stress: "More than one primary stress may occur in a stretch between contours. Stresses become louder as the end of a contour approaches, so that the last primary stress is louder than the next-last ..." (p. 9). Word stress: Root morphemes have a single stress; "most affixes have no morphophonemic stress." (p. 29) No rules are given for the location of stress within roots. In most native words stress is realized as primary stress in phrase medial position and if the stressed syllable is phrase final, but as secondary stress if the stressed syllable is other than the last syllable of a phrase final word. For Spanish loans and some native words the reduction to secondary stress only occurs if the word has an internal morpheme boundary. (See p. 24-27 for further details.)
sources.locator: entry 805 Tzeltal, 'STRESS' paragraph, p. 418 (PDF page 3; lines 347-358)
sources.note: Second-hand but page-cited summary of Kaufman 1971 (pp. 9, 12, 24-27, 29), the source Shklovsky 2005 reports as claiming word-initial stress: for Kaufman, word stress is a morphophonemic property of ROOT morphemes (affixes carry none), so it is root stress, not fixed final stress; the root's stress surfaces as primary in phrase-medial position and when phrase-final, but is reduced to secondary when the stressed syllable is not the last syllable of a phrase-final word; loudness increases toward the end of an intonation contour. sources.quote: Cuando el acento mueve de la sílaba última de la raíz 'abat a la última sílaba del sustantivo derivado 'abatél (acuérdese que el tzeltal siempre tiene el acento en la última sílaba), la vocal media queda muy débil.
